title: POC scoping: reserved GPUs & burst/fallback plan - Argentum Labs
summary: Discovery-style scoping focused on sizing reserved capacity for a 6-week POC, burst strategy to handle spiky traffic, fallback policies to hosted Redwood variants, and benchmark plan. Customer requires 50ms token latency SLO for production but will accept higher for POC; SOC2 and KMS questions surfaced. Agreed next step: run a two-day benchmark with sample traffic and share pilot pricing + security pack.
action_items: Maya Patel: Send pilot pricing worksheet and committed-reserved SKU options (due 2027-10-08)
Derek Huang: Provide benchmark harness instructions and starter Locust script + example samples (due 2027-10-09)
Clara Jensen: Share 72-hour sample production traces (anonymized) and typical prompt length distribution (due 2027-10-11)
Ravi Menon: Confirm IP allowlist and VPC peering windows for a 2-day benchmark (due 2027-10-09)
next_steps: Redwood to run a two-day bench with Argentum sample traffic on reserved GPUs + burst to hosted fallback
Customer to review pilot pricing and confirm budget for reserved capacity trial
Security review call scheduled if benchmark is successful to discuss KMS/HSM and audit logging
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Derek (Redwood SE), Jonah (Redwood Solutions), Clara (Argentum Head of ML), Ravi (Infra), Sofia (PM), Tim (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, hi I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this. Derek is our SE, Jonah will help on ops.
[00:12] Clara: Hi all, Clara here. Thanks for squeezing us in.
[00:15] Ravi: Ravi, infra, hello.
[00:17] Sofia: Sofia, product.
[00:19] Tim: Tim, SRE.
[00:24] Derek: Awesome, quick agenda, we want to nail down POC success criteria, how you'll measure, what traffic shape looks like, pick reserved GPU sizing for the 6-week pilot, and design burst + fallback rules. We'll also outline a short benchmark plan.
[00:40] Clara: Great. To set context, Argentum runs a content-moderation inference pipeline, about 1200 qps at peak internal load but bursty with daily spikes. For POC we want to validate cost/latency tradeoffs and confirm we can meet-ish 50-100ms token latency on our top requests. Not strict but it's a goal.
[01:02] Maya: When you say 1200 qps peak, is that across a single model or split?
[01:08] Clara: It's mostly one model for classification then a reranker—about 70% of traffic to the main model, 30% to reranker. Prompt lengths vary; 6-12 tokens for short checks, but 40-60 tokens when we attach context. Average output length is 16 tokens.
[01:30] Derek: Okay, that helps. For POC we usually recommend sizing for peak sustained throughput you expect during the two-day bench. Do you have a 95th percentile qps for the last 30 days?
[01:44] Ravi: Our telemetry's messy, but 95th steady-state is around 600 qps, peaks up to 1200 for short bursts.
[01:53] Jonah: For reserved GPUs we map that into per-GPU throughput based on model and token/service. What model family are you planning?
[02:02] Clara: We'll test with an open LLM we vetted, similar to Llama-3-13B quantized. We're open to testing Redwood-verified variants too.
[02:12] Derek: Perfect. Rough math: on A100-like hardware with q8 quantization we see ~250 tokens/sec per GPU for that model architecture under typical configs, but latency depends on batching and KV cache hit rates. If your avg response is 16 tokens, that's roughly 15-20 requests per second per GPU at low batching. But with continuous batching you can get higher throughput.
[02:40] Sofia: So for 600qps steady you'd need ~30 GPUs? That seems high.
[02:47] Derek: The numbers vary a lot—depends how much batching you accept. Also, Redwood supports dedicated pooling and autoscaling policies. For POC we often do a hybrid: reserve a base pool sized for 95th steady-state (to keep predictable latency), plus burst headroom that can spin up against dedicated leftover capacity or fall back to hosted variants.
[03:08] Maya: To avoid surprises, a common pattern is reserve 8-12 GPUs for the POC, run the benchmark, and then iterate. The benchmark will show your effective RPS per GPU with your exact prompt shapes and prefix cache hit rate.
[03:20] Clara: That feels reasonable. Our budget is a factor—what's the pricing delta for reserved vs. on-demand?
[03:27] Maya: We'll send the pilot pricing worksheet, but ballpark reserved gives 30-40% discount vs on-demand; dedicated reserved also guarantees capacity for the window. For a short 6-week pilot we can propose a simple committed SKU.
[03:41] Tim: On fallback, we need deterministic behavior if the reserved pool is saturated—no silent errors. We prefer automatic reroute to a slightly cheaper hosted variant with explicit latency/cost tradeoff. Is that supported?
[03:52] Derek: Yes. Redwood's routing can be policy-driven: prefer reserved pool, if queue depth hits threshold or latency anomaly occurs, route to hosted model variant or a smaller model. We can also return a specific response header so your app knows it was served by fallback.
[04:10] Clara: Good. Also audit logs and KMS — we need to know how data is handled during POC; audit and encryption are critical.
[04:19] Maya: We'll include the security pack (SOC2 attestation summary, KMS integration guide, audit logging details). For POC we recommend using a customer-managed KMS for any sensitive keys; if you can't we can provide logs and a scoped data retention policy.
[04:34] Ravi: For the benchmark we need to open a peering window and allow IPs — probably a 48-hour window. We'll confirm the list.
[04:42] Derek: Noted. For the two-day bench, our plan: run three profiles — steady at 600 qps, high-burst scenario with sustained 1.2k qps for 10-minute windows every hour, and a ramp test to observe queuing behavior. We'll collect latency P50/P95/P99 per token, tokens/sec per GPU, CPU/GPU utilization, and KV cache hit rates.
[05:05] Sofia: What's your suggested queue depth threshold to trigger fallback?
[05:10] Derek: We usually set a conservative soft-queue at 40ms above SLO or queue depth > N requests per GPU (we'll provide the numbers after initial bench). For POC you can start with a fallback trigger of average latency > 120ms for 30s or queue > 100 total.
[05:29] Tim: Would fallback cause double spend (billing) or any request duplication? We need idempotency guarantees.
[05:35] Derek: No duplication — Redwood's routing will only call one backend. If the reserved pool can't accept, request is routed. We'll surface metrics about where it was served. Billing is per token at the service that served it; we'll include pilot pricing that models fallback costs.
[05:50] Clara: For our success criteria: 1) prove we can handle 600qps steady with P95 response under 150ms token latency, 2) cost estimate < X per 1M tokens (we'll fill X after internal), 3) no data exfil events and logged KMS key usage. If these hold we move to reserved in prod.
[06:12] Maya: Good, let's codify. For the POC sizing hypothesis we propose reserved base of 10 GPUs (q8 quant) to start. During the bench we'll confirm if that's sufficient. If we see sustained saturation we'll recommend incremental reserve or change to split routing with a reranker on smaller instances.
[06:31] Ravi: 10 GPUs is within our comfortable budget for six weeks. Can you give a rough timeline to get the bench running after we share traces?
[06:39] Jonah: Once we receive traces and IP peering windows, we can spin up the reserved pool and run a smoke test in 48 hours, full two-day bench within 72 hours after that. So basically within a week.
[06:52] Sofia: What about KV caching — we have a lot of repeated prefixes; how do you recommend we configure cache to reduce cost?
[06:58] Derek: We'll enable prefix/KV caching in Redwood Optimize. The benchmark will report hit rates. If hit rates are >30% you can see significant token cost savings and reduced per-request latency. We'll also test a cold/warm start scenario.
[07:12] Clara: On model variants — can we fall back to a quantized 7B variant hosted in region to keep latency low?
[07:18] Derek: Yes, that's a standard fallback: route to a lower-footprint variant in the same region. It preserves availability, lowers cost, and if you configure a threshold you can mark those responses in metadata. Some language differences possible; we'll include evaluation prompts to measure quality delta.
[07:34] Tim: For canary and rollouts after POC, do you support percent-based traffic splits and gradual ramping?
[07:40] Maya: Yes — Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, percent splits, and automatic fallback on regressions. For production we'll work with you to design the rollout policy.
[07:49] Clara: One more thing — our compliance team needs a list of encryption in transit and at rest details.
[07:55] Maya: We'll attach the security pack. Also, if you prefer, we can schedule a 30-minute security deep-dive with our security engineer.
[08:02] Ravi: Let's do that after the benchmark if things look good.
[08:06] Derek: Notes on benchmarks — please include example tokenization and prompt distributions. Small differences in tokenization can change token counts; we'll normalize on one tokenizer during the bench.
[08:16] Sofia: We'll send the anonymized traces and prompt set by Monday.
[08:20] Maya: Great. I'll send the pilot pricing by Friday, Derek will send the benchmark harness and example Locust config tomorrow.
[08:29] Clara: For the POC success criteria, can we capture a guardrail: "if P99 latency > 400ms during steady-state we stop and re-evaluate"?
[08:38] Derek: Absolutely — we can set hard SLO stop conditions in the bench orchestration to protect your downstream systems.
[08:45] Mia: (background) sorry, Mia is late.
[08:47] Jonah: small note on autoscaling — Redwood Dedicated autoscaler can scale based on queue depth or GPU utilization; for POC we recommend queue-depth based to avoid latency spikes for quick bursts.
[08:59] Tim: Sounds good. Regarding logs, we need request-level ids retained for 30 days. Is that possible?
[09:05] Maya: Yes, we can support requested retention for the POC and provide an export of logs, subject to agreed PII redaction.
[09:12] Clara: Anything else on fallback? We want deterministic downgrade rather than random.
[09:18] Derek: We'll use explicit policy: reserved preferred, if queue > threshold OR latency exceeds threshold for more than X seconds then route to fallback. Fallback options include hosted same-model quantized, smaller-model local region, or queued-with-backoff mode with explicit 503 styled responses.
[09:35] Sofia: Okay, recap and next steps please.
[09:39] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pilot pricing, security pack, benchmark harness. Argentum to send anonymized traces and confirm IP peering windows. Redwood runs 2-day bench on reserved 10 GPU hypothesis, measuring P50/P95/P99 token latency, tokens/sec per GPU, KV cache hit. After bench we'll review results and schedule security/deep dive.
[09:58] Clara: Thanks, that's perfect.
[10:02] Maya: We'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench window. Thanks everyone.
[10:08] End of transcript.
